questionText:
Read the passage and answer the question:
 
 
 Gandhi’s Salt March
 
The Salt March was notable for at least three reasons. First, it was this
event that first brought Mahatma Gandhi to world attention. Second, it was
the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers.
A woman socialist activist had persuaded Gandhiji not to restrict the
protests to men alone. Third, and perhaps most significant, was the Salt
March, which forced upon the British the realization that their Raj would
not last forever, and that they would have to devolve some power to the
Indians. To that end, the British government convened a series of “Round
Table Conferences” in London. The first meeting was held in November
1930 but without the pre-eminent political leader in India, thus rendering it
an exercise in futility. Gandhiji was released from jail in January 1931. A
Second Round Table Conference was held in London in the latter part of
1931. Here, Gandhiji represented the Congress. However, his claims that
his party represented all of India came under challenge from three parties:
from the Muslim League, which claimed to stand for the interests of the
Muslims, from the Princes, and from the brilliant lawyer and thinker B.R.
Ambedkar, who argued that Gandhiji and the Congress did not really
represent the lower castes.
Name the leader who represented the Indian National Congress at the
Second Round Table Conference in London:

questionText:
Read the passage and answer the questions:
 The
Making and Unmaking of the Non-Cooperation
During the Great War of 1914–18, the British had instituted censorship of
the press and permitted detention without trial. Now, on the
recommendation of a committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, these
tough measures were continued. In response, Gandhiji called for a
countrywide campaign against the “Rowlatt Act”. In towns across North
and West India, life came to a standstill, as shops shut down and schools
closed in response to the bandh call. The protests were particularly intense
in the Punjab, where many men had served on the British side in the War –
expecting to be rewarded for their service. Instead they were given the
Rowlatt Act. Gandhiji was detained while proceeding to the Punjab. The
situation in the province grew progressively more tense, reaching a bloody
climax in Amritsar in 1919, when a British Brigadier ordered his troops to
open fire on a nationalist meeting. More than four hundred people were
killed in what is known as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. It was the
Rowlatt satyagraha that made Gandhiji a truly national leader. Emboldened
by its success, Gandhiji called for a campaign of “non-cooperation” with
British rule. Indians who wished colonialism to end were asked to stop
attending schools, colleges and law courts, and not pay taxes. In sum, they
were asked to adhere to a “renunciation of (all) voluntary association with
the (British) Government”. If non-cooperation was effectively carried out,
said Gandhiji, India would win swaraj within a year.

was:

After the failure of the Cripps Mission, Mahatma Gandhi decided to launch his third major movement against British rule. This was the "Quit India" campaign, which began in August 1942. Although Gandhiji was jailed at one point, younger activists organised strikes and acts of sabotage across the country. Particularly active in the underground resistance were socialist members of the Congress, such as Jayaprakash Narayan. In several districts, such as Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east, "independent" governments were proclaimed. "Quit India" was genuinely a mass movement, bringing into its ambit hundreds of thousands of ordinary Indians. It especially energised the young who, in very large numbers, left their colleges to go to jail. In June 1944, with the end of the war in sight, Gandhiji was released from prison.

questionText:
Read the following excerpt carefully and answer the question that follows:

"On 2 March 1930, Mahatma Gandhi addressed a letter to Viceroy Lord Irwin explaining why he had chosen the salt tax as the target of Civil Disobedience: 'If you cannot see your way to deal with these evils and my letter makes no appeal to your heart, on the eleventh day of this month I shall proceed with such co-workers of the Ashram as I can take, to disregard the provisions of the Salt Laws. I regard this tax to be the most iniquitous of all from the poor man's standpoint. As the Independence movement is essentially for the poorest in the land, the beginning will be made with this evil. Salt is an article of prime necessity to the poorest human and cattle; its tax falls with crushing severity on the poor, while the state monopoly deprives millions of coastal villagers of their natural right to manufacture salt freely from the sea.'"

Why did Gandhi denounce the salt tax as the 'most iniquitous of all from the poor man's standpoint'?

options.text: Because salt was used exclusively by wealthy British aristocrats
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: Because salt manufacturing required expensive imported British coal
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: Because salt could be replaced by sugarcane molasses
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

options.text: Because salt was a vital, universal necessity for both humans and cattle, and the tax fell disproportionately heavily upon the poorest families
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately identifies the verified NCERT concept for Gandhi's Ultimatum to Lord Irwin (March 1930).

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT principles for Mahatma Gandhi and National Movement (Gandhi's Ultimatum to Lord Irwin (March 1930)):
Because salt was a vital, universal necessity for both humans and cattle, and the tax fell disproportionately heavily upon the poorest families

Detailed Context:
1. Salt was essential for basic biological survival; taxing it meant taxing the daily bread of the most impoverished citizens.
Hence Option B is correct.

Therefore, option (D) is the correct answer.
